candidates.research_question: Why does the ISS-type light-scattering detector miss many Kapton and Teflon pyrolysis smokes, why did its response change between SAME and SAME-R, and do multi-property detectors close this gap under spacecraft flow and aging conditions?
candidates.why_it_matters: Kapton and Teflon are abundant in spacecraft electrical systems, where fires are likely to begin; the ISS detector is the state of the art for spacecraft fire detection, and the Gateway HALO threshold was derived from tests that include these materials.
candidates.evidence_gap: Within the examined sources, the cause of the SAME/SAME-R difference is unexplained, and no next-generation detector has been evaluated for alarm performance against Kapton and Teflon smoke in microgravity (the MPASS prototype estimated concentration only).
candidates.uncertainty: Few runs per campaign; the 2.0 V threshold is derived from a figure line; Figure 9 per-run values are not digitised; denominators of the published 'over half' / 'two thirds' are unknown.

candidates.research_question: How do elevated oxygen (30-34% O2) and reduced pressure (8.2-10.2 psi) change pre-fire smoke particles and the response of heritage and candidate detectors?
candidates.why_it_matters: Planned lunar habitats and Gateway run at reduced pressure with elevated oxygen, which raises material flammability and is expected to change smoke emission and detector behaviour.
candidates.evidence_gap: Within the examined sources, pyrolysis smoke and spacecraft smoke detectors were tested only in ordinary air at 14.7 psi; Saffire IV-VI covered flaming fires at exploration-like atmospheres with an assumed alarm threshold.
candidates.uncertainty: The SAME/SAME-R atmosphere is inferred from the glovebox facility description; Saffire results are for flaming fires in one vehicle geometry.

candidates.research_question: How does lunar gravity change smoke particle growth, plume transport and the best detector placement in a habitat whose airflow is also designed for dust control?
candidates.why_it_matters: Buoyancy returns at lunar gravity, so smoke transport and the best detector location differ from both the ISS and Earth; this drives detector placement and alarm timing for Artemis surface systems.
candidates.evidence_gap: Within the examined sources, no smoke or detector measurement exists in partial gravity; detector placement has been studied only by simulation.
candidates.uncertainty: Extrapolating from microgravity and 1 g data to lunar gravity is a hypothesis for smoke transport and detection; planned lunar experiments are combustion-focused.

candidates.research_question: Can a detector separate fire smoke from cabin and lunar dust, and what is the actual false-alarm behaviour of heritage detectors under controlled dust exposure?
candidates.why_it_matters: Dust false alarms lead crews to switch detectors off during cleaning, and lunar dust overlaps smoke in size and may be far more concentrated than ISS dust, so detection could be lost for long periods on the Moon.
candidates.evidence_gap: Within the examined sources, false alarms are known only from operational reports and no controlled dust test of the heritage detectors was found; discriminating detectors are early prototypes.
candidates.uncertainty: No public ISS false-alarm database; lunar dust loads in NASA-STD-1008 are conservative estimates.

candidates.research_question: What smoke do understudied spacecraft fuels (lithium-ion batteries, Artemis crew fabrics, PMMA, Nomex) produce, and which detectors sense it in microgravity?
candidates.why_it_matters: Laptop battery fires are among the most likely long-mission fire scenarios, and new lunar fabrics and common polymers were never part of the microgravity detector tests.
candidates.evidence_gap: Within the examined sources, the heritage detectors were tested in microgravity with five pyrolysis smokes only; PMMA has one 1 g exposure and battery smoke none.
candidates.uncertainty: Material lists in the examined sources may not be exhaustive.

candidates.research_question: How do heritage and candidate detectors respond to flaming-fire smoke in microgravity, and can an alarm threshold be set low enough to alarm before carbon monoxide becomes hazardous?
candidates.why_it_matters: In Saffire VI an assumed 2 mg/m3 threshold alarmed only after CO exceeded the 24-hour exposure limit in both PMMA fires, and cabin filtration can keep smoke from building up while toxic gases accumulate.
candidates.evidence_gap: Within the examined sources, the ISS and Shuttle detectors were never exposed to flaming-fire smoke in microgravity, and the Saffire threshold analysis used an assumed alarm point.
candidates.uncertainty: Two Saffire VI PMMA tests in one uncrewed vehicle; vehicle-specific mixing strongly affects time to alarm.
